In three weeks in early 2014, Crimea went from Ukrainian to Russian without a declared war — just soldiers without insignia, and a vote held under their guns.

a thread 🧭🗺️

1/ It starts February 27, 2014, days after Ukraine's president fled Kyiv. Armed men in unmarked uniforms — soon nicknamed ‘little green men’ — seized Crimea's parliament and airports. Russia denied they were its troops. Putin later admitted they were.

2/ By March 1 Russian forces held most of the peninsula. Kyiv's new government had no real way to contest it — Ukraine's own troops in Crimea were surrounded, cut off from orders, and never told to fight.

3/ On March 16 a referendum asked Crimeans to choose Russia or Ukraine — staying with Ukraine as it was wasn't on the ballot. Official count: 95.5% for Russia, turnout 83%. Independent estimates put real support and turnout both lower, and Crimean Tatars mostly boycotted.

4/ March 18: Russia and the newly declared 'Republic of Crimea' signed a treaty of accession. March 21: Russia's parliament ratified it, making Crimea and Sevastopol federal subjects of Russia — two new regions on paper, in three weeks.

5/ The rest of the world didn't follow along. The UN General Assembly voted 100-11 to call the referendum invalid. Ukraine, the US, the EU and most countries still list Crimea as Ukrainian territory under occupation, not as Russian soil.

6/ Over a decade later, almost no one recognises the annexation, but no war has reversed it. Crimea sits in an odd category: unrecognised internationally, unmoved practically.
